Most of the galaxies
you can see through
a telescope are already
out of reach.
Not for now.
Forever.
Even a ship traveling
at the speed of
light could never get there.
And the reason is
one of the strangest
facts in all of physics.
Start with the speed limit.
Light travels at about
186,000 miles per second,
and according to Einstein,
it is the universal
speed limit of cause
and effect.
Nothing with mass can
ever exceed it,
or even reach it.
That alone makes the
universe enormous for us.
But it is not
what seals us in.
What seals us in
is the expansion of space.
Galaxies are not really
flying through space like
bullets.
Instead, the fabric of
space itself is stretching
between them.
Between you and a
distant galaxy, new cubic
light-years of empty space
keep appearing, every single
moment.
And Hubble's Law tells
us that the speed
at which a galaxy
recedes is proportional
to its distance.
Twice as far away,
twice as fast.
Now connect the dots.
At a distance of
about 14 billion light-years
from Earth, the space
between us and those
regions is growing faster
than light.
Does that break Einstein's
rule?
No.
Relativity says nothing
can move through space
faster than light.
It says nothing about
how fast space itself
can stretch.
Imagine running on a
giant treadmill.
Your top speed is
10 miles per hour,
but the belt beneath
you moves backward at
20, then 50,
then 100 miles per hour.
No matter how hard
you run, you are
dragged backward.
For a beam of
light trying to reach
the most distant galaxies,
the cosmic treadmill moves
faster than its top speed.
The true point of
no return lies at
roughly 16 billion
light-years.
It is called the
cosmic event horizon.
Any galaxy beyond it
is cut off from
us for good.
A beam of light
fired toward those regions
right now would travel
forever and never arrive.
And here is the
part that hurts.
By one widely cited
estimate, even a ship
launched at the speed
of light today could
never reach about 94
percent of the galaxies
in the observable universe.
We can look at them.
We can photograph them
and study their past.
But we can never touch them.
So where is the
real edge of the
universe, and why are
we trapped inside it?
The full story is
on Miya's Lab.
